text: Multi-cloud isn't a strategy you adopt because two providers sound safer than one. The organizations that genuinely end up running more than one cloud almost always got there for a short list of concrete reasons, not because someone in an architecture review decided it was a good idea in the abstract. This lesson walks through the real drivers, and the one reason that shows up constantly in decks but almost never survives an honest cost analysis.

The most common path is inheritance: an acquisition brings in a company that already built its stack on a different cloud, and multi-cloud arrives as a fact on day one of integration, not a chosen strategy. The second is a genuine best-of-breed gap — a specific capability one provider closes meaningfully better for a specific workload, where the value justifies the integration cost. The third is disaster-recovery independence: for regulated or existential workloads, running on two providers so an outage or account issue at one can't take down the business. All three are concrete, specific, and defensible.

Now contrast those with the reason that doesn't hold up: 'we don't want to be locked into one vendor,' offered with no specific workload, no specific capability gap, and no specific scenario attached. Ask the follow-up question — locked in to what, exactly, and what's the actual plan if that happens? If nobody in the room can answer with a named service and a named cost comparison, the proposal isn't a requirement. It's an anxiety, and building architecture around an anxiety tends to buy real, ongoing operational cost against a risk that may never materialize.

So before any workload gets a second cloud provider, run it through three questions. What specific capability, constraint, or event is actually driving this request? What does running it on two providers really cost, once you count duplicated tooling, duplicated skill, and duplicated security and monitoring posture, not just infrastructure spend? And is there a cheaper way to get the same protection — a portable pattern, a single-cloud multi-region design, or a contractual hedge instead of an architectural one? If question one can't be answered concretely, you already have your answer.

Once a workload has a genuine, named reason to span two clouds, the next decision is what shape that multi-cloud takes — picking the best service per workload, or deliberately duplicating a workload for resilience. Those are very different commitments with very different costs, and that's exactly where Lesson 6 picks up.
